title: A topological homotopy equivalence induces all homotopy-group isomorphisms
statement: Use the continuous cubical homotopy-group and path-component conventions of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], spelled out below for arbitrary topological spaces. Let $X,Y$ be topological spaces and let $f:X\to Y$, $g:Y\to X$ be continuous maps. Suppose there are continuous maps $H:X\times[0,1]\to X$ and $K:Y\times[0,1]\to Y$ with $H(x,0)=g(f(x))$, $H(x,1)=x$, $K(y,0)=f(g(y))$, and $K(y,1)=y$, using ordinary product topologies. Then $f$ induces a bijection between the sets of path components of $X$ and $Y$. For every $x\in X$ and every integer $n\geq1$, postcomposition induces a group isomorphism $f_*:\pi_n(X,x)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_n(Y,f(x))$. Here $\pi_n(X,x)$ consists of homotopy classes relative to the boundary of continuous maps $([0,1]^n,\partial[0,1]^n)\to(X,x)$, with multiplication by concatenation in the first coordinate, and $f_*[u]=[f\circ u]$. The homotopies $H,K$ need not fix any basepoint. Neither connectedness nor nonemptiness is assumed.

source.place: Algebraic Topology, section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342 (PDF pp. 5–6), change-of-basepoint maps and the paragraph immediately before Proposition 4.1: homotopy equivalences induce homotopy-group isomorphisms even for nonstationary basepoints. Read online; archival copy WANTED. This is a topological theorem, not a Stacks-tag claim.

proof.text: Postcomposition with $f$ and $g$ gives well-defined functions $F_0:\pi_0(X)\to\pi_0(Y)$ and $G_0:\pi_0(Y)\to\pi_0(X)$: a path between two points is sent to a path between their images. For each $z\in X$, $t\mapsto H(z,t)$ is a path from $g(f(z))$ to $z$, so $G_0F_0([z])=[z]$. Likewise $t\mapsto K(w,t)$ gives $F_0G_0([w])=[w]$ for every $w\in Y$. Thus $F_0$ is a bijection with inverse $G_0$. This argument is valid also for empty spaces: if one space is empty then the existence of both $f$ and $g$ forces the other to be empty.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 340, path-component convention; agent expansion of the inverse-on-components argument

proof.text: Fix $x\in X$ and $n\geq1$. Put $A=\pi_n(X,x)$, $B=\pi_n(Y,f(x))$, $C=\pi_n(X,g(f(x)))$, and $D=\pi_n(Y,f(g(f(x))))$. Let $a:A\to B$, $b:B\to C$, and $c:C\to D$ be postcomposition by $f$, $g$, and $f$, respectively, at these specified basepoints. These are well-defined homomorphisms: composing a relative-boundary homotopy with the continuous map gives a relative-boundary homotopy, and postcomposition commutes pointwise with the two pieces of concatenation in the first coordinate. Direct composition of representatives gives $ba=(gf)_{*,x}$, $cb=(fg)_{*,f(x)}$, and the identity map of a space induces the identity group homomorphism.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 342, functoriality of homotopy groups; agent expansion of the representative calculation

proof.text: Notation for steps 3–6: $D=[0,1]^n$, $c=(\tfrac12,\ldots,\tfrac12)$ and $r(u)=2\max_i|u_i-\tfrac12|$, so $0\leq r\leq1$ and $r(u)=1$ exactly on $\partial D$. A function on $D$ or on $[0,1]\times D$ that is continuous on each of two closed sets covering it is continuous: the inverse image of a closed set is the union of two sets closed in closed subsets. For a space $T$, a path $\gamma:[0,1]\to T$ from $t_0$ to $t_1$ and a representative $a:(D,\partial D)\to(T,t_1)$, define $\beta_\gamma a$ by $a(c+2(u-c))$ on $r(u)\leq\tfrac12$ and by $\gamma(2-2r(u))$ on $r(u)\geq\tfrac12$. On the first region $c+2(u-c)\in D$; on the seam $r=\tfrac12$ this point lies on $\partial D$, so both formulas give $t_1=\gamma(1)$; hence $\beta_\gamma a$ is continuous, and on $\partial D$ it equals $\gamma(0)=t_0$. Replacing $a$ by a homotopy $a_s$ relative to $\partial D$ in the inner formula gives a homotopy relative to $\partial D$ of the results. Thus $\beta_\gamma:\pi_n(T,t_1)\to\pi_n(T,t_0)$ is a well-defined function.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 341, change-of-basepoint map; agent expansion with explicit shell formula

proof.text: Collar identity. Let $F:[0,1]\times D\to T$ be continuous with $F(t,u)=\gamma(t)$ for all $u\in\partial D$. Put $\lambda(t)=1-t/2\in[\tfrac12,1]$, and define $B(t,u)=F(t,c+(u-c)/\lambda(t))$ on $r(u)\leq\lambda(t)$ and $B(t,u)=\gamma(2-2r(u))$ on $r(u)\geq\lambda(t)$. Both regions are closed and cover $[0,1]\times D$. On the first region $r(c+(u-c)/\lambda(t))=r(u)/\lambda(t)\leq1$, so the point lies in $D$; on the second $0\leq2-2r(u)\leq t\leq1$. On the seam $r(u)=\lambda(t)$ the rescaled point lies on $\partial D$ and $2-2r(u)=t$, so both formulas give $\gamma(t)$. By step 3's pasting rule $B$ is continuous. For $u\in\partial D$, $B(t,u)=\gamma(0)$ (when $t=0$ use $F(0,u)=\gamma(0)$). At $t=0$, $\lambda=1$ and $B(0,-)=F(0,-)$; at $t=1$, $\lambda=\tfrac12$ and $B(1,-)=\beta_\gamma(F(1,-))$, where $F(1,-)$ is based at $\gamma(1)$. Hence $[F(0,-)]=\beta_\gamma[F(1,-)]$ in $\pi_n(T,\gamma(0))$.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342, homotopies with moving basepoint; agent expansion with explicit collar homotopy

proof.text: $\beta_\gamma$ is a bijection with inverse $\beta_{\overline\gamma}$, $\overline\gamma(s)=\gamma(1-s)$. For $a:(D,\partial D)\to(T,t_1)$ put $\mu(s)=(1+s)/2$ and define $A(s,u)=a(c+(u-c)/\mu(s))$ on $r(u)\leq\mu(s)$ and $A(s,u)=\gamma(s+2-2r(u))$ on $r(u)\geq\mu(s)$. On the second region $s\leq s+2-2r(u)\leq1$; on the seam the rescaled point lies on $\partial D$ and the path argument is $1$, so both formulas give $t_1$. Thus $A$ is continuous, $A(s,u)=\gamma(s)$ for $u\in\partial D$, $A(0,-)=\beta_\gamma a$ and $A(1,-)=a$. Apply step 4 to $F(t,u)=A(1-t,u)$, whose boundary path is $\overline\gamma$ (from $t_1$ to $t_0$): $[a]=\beta_{\overline\gamma}\beta_\gamma[a]$. The same argument with $\overline\gamma$ in place of $\gamma$ gives $[b]=\beta_\gamma\beta_{\overline\gamma}[b]$ for every $[b]\in\pi_n(T,t_0)$. No multiplicativity of $\beta_\gamma$ is used below.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 341, invertibility of change-of-basepoint maps; agent expansion with explicit sweep homotopy

proof.text: Set $\alpha(t)=H(x,t)$, a path in $X$ from $g(f(x))$ to $x$. For a representative $a:(D,\partial D)\to(X,x)$ the map $F(t,u)=H(a(u),t)$ is continuous on $[0,1]\times D$, with $F(t,u)=\alpha(t)$ on $\partial D$, $F(0,-)=g\circ f\circ a$ and $F(1,-)=a$. Step 4 gives $[g\circ f\circ a]=\beta_\alpha[a]$, so with step 2, $ba=(gf)_{*,x}=\beta_\alpha:A\to C$. Likewise $\delta(t)=K(f(x),t)$ is a path in $Y$ from $f(g(f(x)))$ to $f(x)$, and $F(t,u)=K(w(u),t)$ for $w:(D,\partial D)\to(Y,f(x))$ gives $cb=(fg)_{*,f(x)}=\beta_\delta:B\to D$. By step 5 both are bijections, and by step 2 they are homomorphisms; the moving basepoints are retained, and neither composite is treated as an identity map.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 342, nonstationary-basepoint homotopy invariance, and Exercise 4.1.2, printed p. 358; agent application of steps 3–5

proof.text: Since $ba$ is injective, $a$ is injective. Since $cb$ is injective, $b$ is injective. For any $v\in B$, surjectivity of $ba:A\to C$ gives $u\in A$ with $ba(u)=b(v)$, and injectivity of $b$ implies $a(u)=v$. Hence $a$ is surjective and therefore bijective. Its inverse preserves multiplication: if $a(u)=v$ and $a(u')=v'$, then $a(uu')=vv'$, and uniqueness of preimages gives $a^{-1}(vv')=a^{-1}(v)a^{-1}(v')$. Thus the postcomposition homomorphism $a=f_*$ is a group isomorphism for every $x$ and $n\geq1$. The reasoning uses no commutativity, connectedness, or stationary-basepoint assumption.
